title: The city wildlife project
source: Entrevista y preguntas originales de Profesor Particular. Audio con voz sintética en inglés estadounidense.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Today I'm talking to photographer Maya Ellis about her city wildlife project. Maya, you weren't originally planning to photograph animals, were you?

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: No. I was working on a series about old buildings. One afternoon, a child outside a school pointed to a fox crossing an empty playground. I had walked past that place for years without noticing any wildlife. That moment made me curious about what else I was missing. It wasn't a college assignment, and nobody had asked me to start a new project.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: What was hardest when you began?

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: I expected trouble with the camera because I was using an older model. It was fine. The real difficulty was recognising what I could hear. I would record a sound in a garden and then spend hours discovering whether it was a bird, an insect or even a machine nearby. Once I learned to listen more carefully, I stopped making so many wrong guesses.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Did your way of working change?

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: Quite a lot. At first I visited the same places at lunchtime, when it was convenient for me. But people and traffic made some animals disappear. I began arriving shortly before sunrise instead. I kept using the same locations, so I could compare what I saw at different times. The earlier start was difficult, but it made the photographs much more useful.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: You later invited local volunteers. Did they already know a lot about wildlife?

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: I assumed experienced photographers would contribute the most. In fact, several complete beginners noticed details I had overlooked. One volunteer carefully wrote down where she had seen a small group of birds each morning. Her notes helped us find them again. The volunteers didn't need expensive equipment; their patient observations were the valuable part.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: People share the photographs online. Is that useful?

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: Yes, provided they include some context. A dramatic picture of a fox on a city street can make people think foxes are everywhere, even if it was a rare sight. So when I post an image, I add the date, the place and a short explanation of what happened before and after. I don't want to stop people sharing pictures. I want them to understand what one photograph can and cannot show.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: You also run workshops in schools. What do you hope pupils take away?

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: Some ask whether the workshop will teach them to be professional photographers. That's not its main purpose. We go outside, notice a few things and write down evidence before making a claim. Even if a pupil never picks up a camera again, that habit of careful observation is useful in science and in ordinary life.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: And what happens next for the project?

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: A publisher suggested a book, which was flattering, but that would only show a small selection of images. I'm building a public digital archive where residents can add their own notes beside the photographs. I still have to work out how to check those notes, so it won't launch immediately. But I think a shared record will tell a richer story than a book of my favourite pictures.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Maya Ellis, thank you for joining us.

questions.prompt: Why did Maya begin photographing city wildlife?
options: A school asked her to document its playground.
An unexpected sight made her realise how much she had missed.
She needed a new subject for a college assignment.
questions.why: Un niño le señaló un zorro en un lugar por el que ella había pasado muchas veces; eso despertó su curiosidad.

questions.prompt: What was Maya's main difficulty at the start?
options: Identifying the sounds she recorded.
Finding a camera that worked properly.
Getting permission to visit gardens.
questions.why: Pensó que la cámara antigua daría problemas, pero lo difícil fue distinguir el origen de los sonidos.

questions.prompt: How did Maya change her working routine?
options: She moved to new locations outside the city.
She asked volunteers to photograph the animals for her.
She visited familiar places much earlier in the day.
questions.why: Mantuvo los mismos lugares, pero cambió las visitas del mediodía a poco antes del amanecer.

questions.prompt: What surprised Maya about the volunteers?
options: Beginners noticed useful details that she had missed.
Most owned expensive photographic equipment.
Experienced photographers refused to share notes.
questions.why: Esperaba mucho de los expertos, pero principiantes con notas pacientes aportaron observaciones valiosas.

questions.prompt: What does Maya think about sharing wildlife photographs online?
options: It should be avoided because photographs are misleading.
Pictures are more helpful when accompanied by context.
Only rare animal sightings should be shared.
questions.why: Le parece útil compartirlas si se añaden fecha, lugar y explicación para no exagerar lo que demuestra una sola imagen.

questions.prompt: What is the main aim of Maya's school workshops?
options: To recruit pupils for her photography project.
To train pupils for professional photography.
To develop careful observation before drawing conclusions.
questions.why: Quiere que los alumnos observen y anoten pruebas antes de afirmar algo, aunque no vuelvan a usar una cámara.

questions.prompt: What is Maya planning to do next?
options: Publish a book of her favourite pictures.
Create a digital archive with contributions from residents.
Launch a new exhibition immediately.
questions.why: Descarta por ahora el libro y prepara un archivo digital público con notas aportadas por residentes.
